notes:
Here is a verse‑by‑verse commentary on Matthew 26:1–25, drawn from the sources listed in the instructions. Each point is followed by its source URL.

---

## Matthew 26:1–2 – Jesus Predicts His Death

**v. 1:** *“When Jesus had finished all these sayings, He told His disciples…”*

- The phrase “all these sayings” refers to the Olivet Discourse of Matthew 24–25. In Matthew’s Gospel, this marks the end of Jesus’s public teaching. As Adam Clarke writes, “Having instructed his disciples and the Jews by his discourses, edified them by his example, convinced them by his miracles, he now prepares to redeem them by his blood.”
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-26/

- Ellicott agrees that the words point clearly to the great discourse of Matthew 24–25. The “disciples” may have been the four named in Mark 13:3 or the whole Twelve.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/26.htm

- Gill notes that Jesus was now alone with His disciples; having finished His prophetic office, He was about to enter His priestly office and gives intimations of its near approach.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/matthew/26.htm

**v. 2:** *“You know that the Passover is two days away, and the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified.”*

- Jesus speaks of His betrayal as already accomplished, because it was so certain and near. The “Passover” was the feast commemorating Israel’s deliverance from Egypt; now the true Paschal Lamb was to be slain. Spurgeon says: “Christ our passover would be slain.”
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-26-commentary-spurgeon

- This is the fourth and final time Jesus predicts His arrest and crucifixion (see Mt 16:21; 17:22–23; 20:17–19). The Greek verb *paradidomi* (“handed over”) is in the futuristic present tense, denoting certainty.
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-26-commentary

- The title “Son of Man” is from Daniel 7:13 and is Jesus’ favourite self-designation. Here He focuses the disciples’ attention on His death and does not mention the resurrection.
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-26-commentary

---

## Matthew 26:3–5 – The Plot of the Religious Leaders

**v. 3:** *“At that time the chief priests and elders of the people assembled in the courtyard of the high priest, whose name was Caiaphas…”*

- The meeting was either a formal session of the Sanhedrin or an informal conference of its chief members. Caiaphas had been high priest from A.D. 18 to 36—an extraordinarily long tenure suggesting he had mastered co-operating with the Romans. Annas, his father-in-law, had been deposed but still held influence.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-26/

- Ellicott notes that Caiaphas and his personal adherents were Sadducees, courting Roman favour, while the scribes were mostly Pharisees—a coalition of normally opposed parties.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/26.htm

- Gill: this was the palace or court of the high priest. Assemblies were held in the courts of the nobles.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/matthew/26.htm

**v. 4:** *“…and they conspired to arrest Jesus covertly and kill Him.”*

- The Greek words for “assembled” and “plotted” deliberately echo Psalm 31:13: “while they take counsel together against me, they scheme to take away my life.”
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-26/

- The plan was to take Jesus “by subtilty” (stealth, trickery). The long controversy between Jesus and the religious leaders had finally come to this.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-26/

**v. 5:** *“But not during the feast… or there may be a riot among the people.”*

- They did not want to kill Jesus during Passover for fear of an uproar, yet that is exactly when it happened—a subtle sign that Jesus, not they, controlled events. Jerusalem’s population swelled perhaps fivefold during Passover, and religious and nationalistic fervour ran high.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-26/

- St. Jerome notes that their objection was not from religious scruple but only from fear of a tumult. St. Leo the Great adds that divine Providence overruled them so that the true Lamb would be slain precisely at the Passover feast.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/matthew-26.html

- Spurgeon: “While Jesus was prophesying, his enemies were plotting. Thus was fulfilled Psalm 2:2.”
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-26-commentary-spurgeon

---

## Matthew 26:6–13 – The Anointing at Bethany

**v. 6:** *“While Jesus was in Bethany in the home of Simon the Leper…”*

- All four Gospels place this incident out of strict chronological order. John 12:1 dates it six days before the Passover. Matthew places it here because it connects to Judas’s decision to betray Jesus.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-26/

- Simon “the Leper” was almost certainly someone Jesus had healed; a practising leper could not have hosted a feast. The name stuck to distinguish him from other Simons.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/26.htm

- The Catholic Haydock commentary notes that St. Ambrose thought Simon was still a leper (Christ keeping company with the unclean to purify them), but St. Jerome and Denis the Carthusian argue he had been cured.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/matthew-26.html

**v. 7:** *“…a woman came to Him with an alabaster jar of expensive perfume, which she poured on His head as He reclined at the table.”*

- John 12:3 identifies her as Mary, the sister of Lazarus. Mark and John add that it was pure nard, worth about 300 denarii—roughly a year’s wages for a labourer. The jar was sealed and had to be broken to pour out the contents.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-26/

- Ellicott notes that Jewish ladies commonly wore a perfume flask suspended from a cord round the neck; Mary’s act was extravagant, pouring it all on Jesus’ head, and John adds that it flowed down to His feet.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/26.htm

- Haydock (Catholic): “It is not the use, but the abuse of things, which is blameworthy… A good reputation is a sweet perfume.” (St. Augustine)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/matthew-26.html

**v. 8:** *“When the disciples saw this, they were indignant and asked, ‘Why this waste?’”*

- John 12:4–6 identifies the ringleader as Judas Iscariot, who said this not because he cared for the poor but because he was a thief and keeper of the money bag. The indignation spread to others.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-26/

- Ellicott observes a “singular narrowing of the limits” across the Gospels: Matthew says “the disciples,” Mark “some,” and John names Judas alone. The word for “waste” (*apōleia*) is the same word Jesus uses for Judas as “son of perdition.”
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/26.htm

- Spurgeon: “When you do the best you can do, from the purest motives, and your Lord accepts your service, do not expect that your brethren will approve all your actions.”
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-26-commentary-spurgeon

**v. 9:** *“This perfume could have been sold at a high price, and the money given to the poor.”*

- The estimated value was 300 denarii—enough to feed thousands (cf. John 6:7). St. Thomas Aquinas notes that those disciples who spoke were persuaded either by Judas’s words or by genuine affection for the poor, but Judas’s only motive was avarice.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/matthew-26.html

**v. 10:** *“Aware of this, Jesus asked, ‘Why are you bothering this woman? She has done a beautiful deed to Me.’”*

- The Greek adjective implies more than “good”—it means a noble, honourable work. Jesus defends Mary’s lavish personal devotion. St. John Chrysostom comments that Jesus teaches us not to expect perfect acts of virtue from novices but to protect tender buds of faith.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/matthew-26.html

- Spurgeon: “Is anything wasted which is all for Jesus? It might rather seem as if all would be wasted which was not given to him.”
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-26/

**v. 11:** *“The poor you will always have with you, but you will not always have Me.”*

- Jesus was not discouraging care for the poor (He had just taught the opposite in Matthew 25:31–46). He was highlighting the unique, unrepeatable moment. His bodily presence was about to end.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-26/

- The Catholic Challoner note says: “Me you have not always; viz. in a visible manner, as when conversant here on earth.” This does not contradict Matthew 28:20 (“I am with you always”), which speaks of His spiritual presence.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/matthew-26.html

**v. 12:** *“By pouring this perfume on Me, she has prepared My body for burial.”*

- Jesus interprets Mary’s act as a prophetic anointing for His burial. Kings and priests were anointed, but Jesus says she anointed Him for burial. Even if Mary did not fully understand, her act said what the disciples failed to say.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-26/

- John Calvin writes that Christ confirms the ointment was valued by Him solely in reference to His burial: “He wished to testify by this symbol, that his grave would yield a sweet odor, as it breathed life and salvation through the whole world.”
  — https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom33.ii.xxiv.html

- Ellicott adds that the words must have fallen with strange sadness on the disciples, who were expecting the kingdom to appear immediately. Only Jesus knew His death was near.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/26.htm

**v. 13:** *“Truly I tell you, wherever this gospel is preached in all the world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her.”*

- This remarkable prediction assumes the universal extension of the gospel and has been fulfilled. St. John Chrysostom marvels: “The exploits of kings and emperors are no longer remembered… But when a poor simple woman, in the house of a leper… pours out her ointment; her good work is rehearsed after the lapse of so many ages, in every place of the habitable globe.”
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/matthew-26.html

- Spurgeon adds: “This woman’s outburst of affection… is one of those things which are to live as long as the gospel lives. The aroma of this loving deed is to abide as long as the world itself endures.”
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-26-commentary-spurgeon

## Matthew 26:14–16 – Judas Agrees to Betray Jesus

**v. 14:** *“Then one of the Twelve, the one called Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests…”*

- Matthew places Judas’s decision immediately after the anointing, suggesting the Bethany incident was the final insult for Judas. St. Luke adds that “Satan entered into Judas” (Luke 22:3).
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-26/

- Ellicott ties Judas’s treachery to the anointing: there was the shame and anger of detected guilt, the greed that had been robbed of its expected spoil, and thirst for compensation.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/26.htm

- Spurgeon: “What a contrast to the incident we have just been considering! The anointing of Jesus is to be the theme of admiration wherever the gospel is preached; but his betrayal by Judas will be a subject for execration to all eternity.”
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-26-commentary-spurgeon

**v. 15:** *“…and asked, ‘What are you willing to give me if I hand Him over to you?’ And they set out for him thirty pieces of silver.”*

- Judas’s opening question betrays his motive: money. He did not even mention Jesus’ name. Thirty pieces of silver was the price of a common slave (Exodus 21:31; Zechariah 11:12–13). The low price showed how little value the chief priests placed on Jesus and revealed Judas’s greed.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-26/

- Matthew Poole comments: “Though therefore Judas was covetous enough to have asked more… yet it was thus ordered by the Divine council. Christ must be sold cheap, that he might be the more dear to the souls of the redeemed ones.”
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-26/

- St. Leo the Great (Catholic): “The impious wretch did not betray his divine Master out of fear, but out of avarice. Of all passions the love of sordid lucre is the most vile.”
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/matthew-26.html

- Several motives have been suggested for Judas: (a) resentment as the only Judean among Galileans; (b) disillusionment with a non-political Messiah; (c) concluding Jesus was losing the conflict; (d) a misguided attempt to force Jesus to reveal His power. But Scripture presents only one motivation: greed.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-26/

**v. 16:** *“So from then on Judas looked for an opportunity to betray Jesus.”*

- The deal was struck. Judas now waited and watched for the right moment to hand Jesus over quietly, away from the crowds.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-26/

## Matthew 26:17–19 – Preparing the Passover

**v. 17:** *“On the first day of the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the disciples came to Jesus and asked, ‘Where do You want us to prepare for You to eat the Passover?’”*

- “The first day of the Feast of Unleavened Bread” opens a well-known chronological difficulty: the Synoptics present the Last Supper as the Passover meal, while John seems to place it before the Passover (John 13:1; 18:28). One solution (Adam Clarke) is that Jesus ate the Passover at the beginning of the Jewish day (evening), while most Jews ate at the end of the day—both on the same calendar day but different hours. Another (France) is that Jesus, knowing He would be dead before the regular time, deliberately held the meal one day early.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-26/

- Haydock (Catholic) explains that the Jews began their festivals at sunset of the evening before; the 14th of Nisan was when the lamb was slain, and Christ ate the Pasch after sunset. It also notes that there were different customs: Galileans may have eaten on one day and Judeans on another.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/matthew-26.html

- From Luke 22:7–8 we learn the two sent were Peter and John.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/26.htm

**v. 18:** *“He answered, ‘Go into the city to a certain man and tell him that the Teacher says, “My time is near. I will keep the Passover with My disciples at your house.”’”*

- The “certain man” is unnamed. Mark and Luke add that the disciples would meet a man carrying a water pitcher and follow him to the house. The host was probably a secret disciple (cf. John 12:42). The secrecy may have been to prevent Judas from knowing the location ahead of time.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-26/

- Ellicott: the Greek word (*ton deina*) is used when the writer knows but does not care to name the person. The host would acknowledge “the Teacher’s” authority.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/26.htm

- “My time is near”: to the disciples this may have seemed the long-expected hour of kingdom manifestation, but Jesus meant the time of His suffering and death.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/26.htm

**v. 19:** *“So the disciples did as Jesus had directed them and prepared the Passover.”*

- Preparation involved purchasing the lamb, unleavened bread, bitter herbs, wine, and the conserve of sweet fruits. The Paschal lamb would be slain by a priest in the Temple courts, then roasted. The upper room would be “furnished” with tables arranged as a Roman *triclinium* and cushions.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/26.htm

## Matthew 26:20–25 – The Betrayer Identified

**v. 20:** *“When evening came, Jesus was reclining with the twelve disciples.”*

- “Reclining” (not sitting) was the posture for a formal meal. Since the Jewish day began at sundown, Jesus ate the Passover and was killed on the same calendar day.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-26/

- Ellicott pictures Jesus reclining in the centre, John next to Him leaning on His bosom, Peter on the other side, with the rest arranged in the three groups of four. The washing of feet (John 13) had just occurred.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/26.htm

**v. 21:** *“And while they were eating, He said to them, ‘Truly I tell you, one of you will betray Me.’”*

- The announcement was intentionally vague, designed to provoke self-examination. Ellicott notes that the other disciples had not shared Judas’s specific guilt, but they had joined his murmuring at Bethany and had been quarrelling about precedence—tendencies that could drag them to the same level.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/26.htm

- Spurgeon: “This was a most unpleasant thought to bring to a feast, yet it was most appropriate to the Passover, for God’s commandment to Moses concerning the first paschal lamb was, ‘With bitter herbs they shall eat it.’”
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-26-commentary-spurgeon

- For good reason, Dante’s *Divine Comedy* places Judas in the lowest circle of hell.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-26/

**v. 22:** *“They were deeply grieved and began to ask Him one after another, ‘Surely not I, Lord?’”*

- The form of the Greek question implies expecting a negative answer: “It is not I, is it?” The disciples did not point fingers at one another. Spurgeon calls this “a beautiful trait”—no one said, “Lord, is it Judas?”
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-26/

- John 13:22–26 fills in what Matthew omits: perplexed glances, Peter’s whisper to John, and Jesus giving the dipped morsel to Judas—a by-play unheard or unheeded by the others.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/26.htm

**v. 23:** *“Jesus answered, ‘The one who has dipped his hand into the bowl with Me will betray Me.’”*

- All the disciples dipped from the same bowl, so this did not single out Judas publicly. The point was that the betrayer was a table-companion, a trusted friend—fulfilling Psalm 41:9: “Even my own familiar friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted up his heel against me.”
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-26/

- Trapp: “My fellow-commoner, my familiar friend, Psalm 41:9. This greatly aggravateth the indignity of the matter.”
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-26/

- Ellicott thinks the words were probably spoken to only a few nearest disciples, since Judas later asks the question as if he had not heard them.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/26.htm

**v. 24:** *“The Son of Man will go just as it is written about Him, but woe to that man by whom He is betrayed. It would be better for him if he had not been born.”*

- This is the first direct reference connecting the coming Passion to Old Testament prophecies. Divine sovereignty (“just as it is written”) and human responsibility (“woe to that man”) are held together without contradiction. The appointment of Christ’s suffering did not diminish the guilt of treachery.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/26.htm

- Spurgeon: “A man may get very near to Christ, ay, may dip his hand in the same dish with the Savior, and yet betray him. We may be high in office, and may apparently be very useful, as Judas was; yet we may betray Christ.”
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-26-commentary-spurgeon

**v. 25:** *“Then Judas, who would betray Him, said, ‘Surely not I, Rabbi?’ Jesus answered, ‘You have said it yourself.’”*

- Judas was apparently the last to ask. He used “Rabbi” (Teacher), not “Lord” as the others did—a subtle but telling difference. To ask the question while knowing he had already arranged the arrest was the height of hypocrisy.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-26/

- Spurgeon: “Those who are the last to suspect themselves are usually those who ought to be the first to exercise self-suspicion.”
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-26-commentary-spurgeon

- Jesus’ answer “You have said it” was probably spoken quietly so only Judas heard. Enduring Word suggests Jesus said it not to condemn but to give Judas a final opportunity to repent, “with love in His eyes.”
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-26/

- Haydock (Catholic) notes the answer may have been “spoken in so low a tone of voice, as not perfectly to be heard by all the company,” which explains why Peter later beckoned to John to learn who the betrayer was.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/matthew-26.html

- Matthew’s chiastic structure (per Pett’s Commentary) highlights the contrasts: the disciples call Him “Lord,” are deeply sorry, and ask “Is it I, Lord?”; Judas calls Him “Rabbi,” is the betrayer, and asks “Is it I, Rabbi?”
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/matthew-26.html

## Points of Denominational Distinction

**Roman Catholic view – The chronology and the Eucharist:** Haydock’s commentary stresses that Christ ate the Pasch “after sunset” on the 14th of Nisan according to Mosaic rite, and that the Eucharist was instituted “in unleavened bread, as the Latin Church doth.” The commentary also notes that St. John seems to place the priests’ Passover on a different day, and reconciles this by suggesting Galileans and Judeans observed different days. The Catholic reading also explicitly ties “this is My body” to the doctrine of transubstantiation.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/matthew-26.html

**Reformed view – Calvin on the anointing:** John Calvin emphasises that Christ valued Mary’s ointment not for its fragrance but “solely in reference to his burial”—a figure of the sweet odour of His death that would breathe life through the whole world. He also holds that the three Synoptic accounts (Matthew, Mark, and an unnamed third) are all the same event, against those who multiply anointings.
— https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom33.ii.xxiv.html

**Baptist / Spurgeon – Extravagant devotion:** Spurgeon consistently defends Mary’s “wasteful” act as the height of devotion and draws application for believers: “Go thou, my sister, and do what God bids thee… Obey the holy impulse within thy spirit, my brother; and thou mayest do ten thousand times more than thou hast ever imagined to be possible.” He explicitly contrasts the simplicity of the Lord’s Supper with “the Romish mass.”
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-26-commentary-spurgeon

**Charismatic / Evangelical – Enduring Word (David Guzik):** Guzik emphasises that Jesus was in control of events (the leaders killed Him on the very day they wanted to avoid) and that Mary “understood more because she was in the place of greatest understanding—being at the feet of Jesus.” He also holds that Jesus’ words to Judas (“You have said it”) were an appeal to repentance, spoken with love.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-26/

## Other Views

**Patristic / Orthodox view (St. John Chrysostom):** Chrysostom’s Homily 80 on Matthew treats the anointing woman as distinct from the sinful woman in Luke 7, identifying her as a different person (“one much to be admired, the sister of Lazarus”). He marvels that she came not for bodily healing but “by way of honour only, and for the amendment of the soul.” He also notes that the disciples’ indignation, though misplaced, actually revealed the woman’s munificence by stating the high value (300 pence).
— https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/200180.htm

**Modern scholarship – Chronological difficulties:** Multiple commentators (Carson, France, Bruce, cited at Enduring Word) note the tension between the Synoptic and Johannine chronologies of the Last Supper. The “simplest solution” (France) is that Jesus, knowing He would be dead before the regular time, deliberately held the meal one day early. Others (Clarke) propose that Jesus ate at the beginning of the Jewish day while most Jews ate at the end.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-26/
